prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, and for its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: After the full exchange I keep B006 first, and I have tested the position against the chair's questions. What the lattice clock adds beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes can be stated precisely, and the citation should say it: a magic-wavelength optical lattice in which the light shift of the clock transition cancels, so that thousands of neutral atoms are held Doppler- and recoil-free and interrogated in parallel. That is a different physical idea from the comb, which measures optical frequencies, and from single-ion control, where a single quantum system limits the statistics. The parallel interrogation is what made 10^-18 fractional uncertainty reachable in averaging times short enough to evaluate systematic shifts, and comparisons across millimetre height differences now resolve the gravitational redshift inside one sample. Independent confirmation at several national laboratories means the result does not depend on one group's interpretation. The pair maps onto concept (Katori) and realisation to the extreme (Ye) without a named omission that the committee has to explain away, which is a real advantage when the choice is made in a single year and cannot be revisited. I would anchor the citation on the lattice concept and the 10^-18 demonstration, and keep the comb and ion-clock lineages out of the wording.
statement.case_against: The objection that carries real weight is lineage. Mehlig, Pearce and Eriksson read the lattice clock as a step within territory that the 2005 and 2012 prizes already covered, and Danielsson and Johansson share the worry with less weight. I think the argument on distinct physics answers it, but a reasonable colleague can weigh incremental precision differently, and the redefinition of the second has not happened, so part of the impact is prospective. The credit boundary against Al+ and other ion-clock groups and against the lattice-clock laboratories at NIST, PTB, SYRTE and Tokyo is a judgement call and not zero. And B004 has broader support in the committee: all eight members ranked it, seven in the top three, and four prefer it as first choice. If the committee concludes that a new organising concept should outweigh deployed measurement capability, I would vote for B004 as my first alternative and would not regard that as a poor outcome.

responses.point: Pearce moved from B002 to B004 because colleagues' arguments converged on it, values a sharp prediction that was then falsified and confirmed, and asks whether B006 would overtake B004 once the redefinition of the second is closer.
responses.response: I accept the criterion of a prediction that could fail and was confirmed, and B004 meets it well. B006 meets a parallel criterion, since the claim that magic-wavelength trapping removes the leading systematic shift, and that 10^-18 can be reached with many atoms, was testable and has been tested in several laboratories. On timing I disagree with waiting: the physics prize is for the discovery, not for the metrological decision, and the redefinition of the second would be a consequence that a later citation does not need. The case does not depend on that decision. I would also ask that we do not treat B004's convergence as stronger evidence than it is. Part of it comes from members who moved after reading the other ballots, and that is a reason to check the argument again, not a reason to count it twice.

responses.point: Eriksson sees B004 as a concept that changed what is searched for in band structures, stable through two decades of tests, with a natural theory-plus-experiment credit, and weighs the 2016 overlap as small.
responses.response: I agree that the Z2 classification is a genuine concept and that the 2016 overlap is a weak objection, since the quantum spin Hall physics is distinct from the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz work. My difficulty is the credit boundary that you list yourself. With a three-person limit, Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leave out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who proposed the HgTe route that made the experiment possible, and Zhang's death means the omission cannot be repaired later. A citation limited to the two-dimensional effect and its first observation can narrow the gap but not remove it. For B006 the equivalent question is whether Katori and Ye are complete, and I find that case easier to defend, because the two names correspond to the two steps in the citation and the remaining boundaries are with other clock groups and not with a decisive intermediate step.

responses.point: Mehlig holds B009 first as a rare prediction followed by experimental discovery, argues the pairing mechanism concerns a derived phase and not the discovery, and says waiting for a mechanism may mean waiting indefinitely.
responses.response: That is the strongest form of the B009 case and I take the point that a flat-band citation need not claim the mechanism. My reservation is different from the one in round 1. The experimental half rests on Jarillo-Herrero alone, with Cao and others outside the credited set, and the field's phenomenology is still being separated from twist-angle disorder and strain, which you also note. I would not wait for a mechanism, but I do think a few more years of reproduction will show which of the reported phases are intrinsic, and that matters for how a citation can be worded. I keep B009 as my second alternative and would regard it as a serious candidate in a later year. I still read the clocks' ranking differently from you: a precision gain of two orders of magnitude that opens new tests is a qualitative change, not a number.

responses.point: Olsson names continuity with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as the main objection the committee must answer, discloses her Tokyo and JSPS links and asks the committee to judge recusal on B006.
responses.response: I agree that continuity is the objection to answer, and the answer I propose is the citation wording above: it names the lattice and the 10^-18 demonstration and does not claim the comb or ion control. On recusal, a fellowship at the University of Tokyo and exchanges with Japanese universities, with no collaboration with Katori or Ye, is a connection to minute but not, in my view, a ground for recusal, in the same way as Kroll's stay in Hall's laboratory. I would ask the chair to record both as disclosures and to have the credit of Ye relative to the comb lineage checked once, as the chair proposes, so that the question is closed in the record and not left to later doubt.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the magic-wavelength lattice with parallel interrogation as a new concept or as a precision refinement of the comb and ion-clock lineages; I have given my reasons but cannot show the committee will agree.

Whether ion-clock groups or other lattice-clock laboratories have a claim that makes Katori and Ye look incomplete; I regard it as a boundary question but have not verified individual priority claims beyond what the shortlist supplies.
How much weight B004's broader support should carry against its unresolved Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap, and whether a narrowly worded two-dimensional citation answers it.
Details such as the first demonstration dates and the uncertainty figures are from my own recollection of the field and not from supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B006 (Katori, Ye), B004 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) or B009 (Bistritzer, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero). My documented collaborations are with Anne L'Huillier, the Lund and Keller attosecond groups, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato, none of whom is a credited name on the shortlist. I am a theoretical atomic physicist and therefore professionally close to AMO topics in general, which I note as an affinity and not a conflict. I have read the Kroll and Olsson disclosures and, as before, I do not think either requires recusal on B006.
